listings.name: Old New Orleans Rum Distillery
listings.content: What a cool thing to do in the city that no one has heard of! For a measly ten bucks, you get to tour a rum distillery and have a rum tasting. The guides, who work there, are extremely knowledgeable and ready to impart any information related to the rum process (or simply field questions on what type of rum you should be drinking). The rums are quite high quality too, with several bottles winning international awards yearly. Free van ride from the French Quarter M-F by reservation.

listings.name: Sweet Lorraine's Jazz Club
listings.content: Noted neighborhood jazz venue, just a few blocks from the Frenchmen Street music strip in Marigny. Local modern jazz; they also serve dinners of Creole and soul food 5PM-10PM.

listings.name: Buttermilk Drop
listings.content: 7th Ward sweets bakery with a small sit down space for Creole soul food breakfast and lunch. Baker/owner Mr. Henry used to run Henry's on St. Claude Avenue; loyal customers followed him here.

listings.name: Coco Hut
listings.content: Jamaican/Caribbean. Delivers.

listings.name: McHardy's Chicken & Fixin'
listings.content: Fried chicken is all they do at McHardy's, but they do it right. Pick some up to go.
listings.price: Cheap, just be sure to count your change before you go out the door

listings.name: Poppa's Seafood & Deli
listings.content: A small decent place with meat and crawfish pies, as well as good seafood at very low prices.

listings.name: Sammy's Food Service & Deli
listings.content: A rough neighborhood, but some of the best cheap food in the city. Garlic roast beef po' boys, greasy diner breakfasts done right, crawfish, burgers, fried seafood, etc. It's as far from upscale as you can get, but it's dearly beloved—expect long lines around lunchtime.

listings.name: Stewart's Diner
listings.content: A top-notch soul food diner way off in the uncharted waters of eastern Claiborne Ave. The photos on the wall are a bit amusing—only a truly disaster could have landed G.W. Bush in a place like this! However if there's one thing locals agree with the former president on, it's that places with the fortitude to reopen early after the disaster deserve patronage. It's cheap, and hard to go wrong anywhere on the menu. Cute atmosphere.

listings.name: Bullet's Sports Bar
listings.content: Not quite as rough as the name might suggest. Sometimes hosts live jazz combos, including local favorite Kermit Ruffins - this is a more intimate venue than the more famous jazz halls visitors are likely to catch him at.

listings.name: No Dice
listings.content: Local bar with more of a Marigny than 7th Ward vibe; also has live music and other events some evenings.

listings.name: St Roch Tavern
listings.content: This is the sort of edgy dive where you will leave with both a strong impression and an opinion of the place. New Orleans bounce rules most nights, but Sa nights past 1AM turn into a punk party with plenty of dancing. Other times there may be brass bands, R&B, and other eclectic local entertainment. Otherwise, it's just a real dive of a place, with regulars who may or may not be friendly... Drinks are real cheap, the Mexican food is a nice change of bar food pace, there is occasional free red beans and rice, and there are a bunch of dogs milling about at virtually all hours.

listings.name: Mount Olivet Episcopal Church
listings.content: This, Algiers' oldest structure, and one of the few to survive the Great Algiers Fire, dates back to 1845. While the exterior is charming, the interior is nothing terribly exciting. Just around the corner on Olivier is another interesting old columned building—this one a former Masonic house.

listings.name: Old Courthouse
listings.content: This hulking Romanesque building is the most obvious landmark upon arriving on the shores of the West Bank, and is still functioning both as a courthouse and office space for several local government facilities. While the original courthouse dated back to 1812 in its first incarnation as a plantation home, the current building was built following the Great Algiers Fire in 1896.

listings.name: Dimartino's Famous Muffulettas
listings.content: The famous muffuletta sandwich is the star attraction at DiMartino's, a small local chain that also has plenty of Cajun and Creole options, plus great burgers.

listings.name: Tout de Suite Cafe
listings.content: Coffee, pastries, fresh made panini sandwiches, and WiFi. Great old Algiers atmosphere.

listings.name: Seafood Zone
listings.content: Strip mall dive eatery but with tasty gumbo and other seafood entrees.

listings.name: Algiers Sports Bar
listings.content: A good laid-back place for some Abita with older locals, and a few rounds of pool.

listings.name: Crown & Anchor
listings.content: Algiers Point's best known and most popular bar is an authentic-enough English-style pub, with lively darts games and friendly locals. The beer is pricey, but nonetheless, this is a great and straightforward destination on a weekend jaunt across the river.

listings.name: Dry Dock Cafe
listings.content: This place will serve you expensive beer and basic and cheap New Orleans fare (until 10PM) in a casual, but nicer-than-your-average-dive bar atmosphere. A bit on the average side, though locally popular.

listings.name: Old Point Bar
listings.content: Nice old style bar, also Algier's leading live music venue, showcasing a variety of local talent. If you haven't heard of a performer listed here, don't worry, they're probably good. Comfortable old road house atmosphere. Early shows on Sundays.

listings.name: House of the Rising Sun B&B
listings.content: There is a house, down in New Orleans... This shotgun house, though, is likely more comfortable than the one of ill-repute in the song. The owner is a huge music fan with exhaustive knowledge of local jazz musicians and local jazz history, and is an excellent resource if you are looking to learn a bit, or just to find good spots for live jazz during your stay.

listings.name: Audubon Park
listings.content: Pleasant park to walk around, designed by Frederick Law Olmsted, the same fellow who designed Central Park in New York City. Runs from St. Charles Avenue to the river.

listings.name: Audubon Zoo
listings.content: Very good zoo, see the rare white alligators, at the upper end of Magazine Street. Riverboats connect the Zoo to the Central Business District; also accessible from the St. Charles Streetcar via a shuttle bus that runs back and forth from the main entrance to Audubon Park on St. Charles to the Zoo.

listings.name: Cascade Stables
listings.content: Horse stables, riding lessons.

listings.name: Tulane University
listings.content: The main campus of New Orleans' most famous university stretches from St. Charles Avenue across from Audubon Park back to Claiborne Avenue. It includes a few attractions of special interest to some:

listings.name: Tulane Jazz Archive
listings.content: New Orleans jazz fans can see a display of photographs and artifacts, and research by reading or listening to interviews with historic jazz musicians.

listings.name: Middle American Research Institute
listings.content: With a major renovation of Dinwiddie Hall being completed, the pre-Columbian artifacts are not on public display at writing but will return in 2012. However a few items are on display elsewhere on campus, and the Institute sponsors special events. Lovers of ancient Meso-America should check the website for details.

listings.name: Uptown Crescent City Farmers Market
listings.content: Market with fresh produce and fresh prepared local dishes. Every Tuesday 9AM-1PM, University Square parking lot (formerly known as Uptown Square), 200 block of Broadway, near the riverfront, a couple blocks on the upriver side of Audubon Park.

listings.name: Crepes à la Carte
listings.content: Fresh made sweet or savory crepes for a meal or snack. Has a small bench and when the weather is good a couple of little outdoor tables, but most business is "to go"; the crepes come in a convenient paper cone so they can be eaten while walking.

listings.name: Felipe's Taqueria
listings.content: Popular location of small chain; fresh made Mexican

listings.name: Café Freret
listings.content: Tables are shaded under a roof but not walled in. "Pet friendly" if you're looking for a place to eat with your dog. Prices reasonable, though service can be slow.

listings.name: Naked Pizza
listings.content: Pizza with all natural healthy ingredients; even vegan and gluten free options. The original location of what has become a growing franchise. Take out or delivery.

listings.name: Pyramids Cafe
listings.content: Middle Eastern. Eat in or delivery.

listings.name: Ted's Frostop
listings.content: Old school style burgers, shakes, fries & rootbeer. Also simple breakfasts.

listings.name: Wing Zone
listings.content: Branch of chain, chicken wings, chicken fingers, burgers

listings.name: Kupcake Factory
listings.content: Cupcakes and gelato

listings.name: First Cup Cafe
listings.content: Nice small coffee house, free Wi-Fi for paying customers.

listings.name: PJ's Coffee & Tea
listings.content: 2 locations of popular local chain on the Tulane campus; 6501 Willow (Willow Hall); and in the breezeway of Stern Hall on Freret at McAlister.

listings.name: Audubon Clubhouse Cafe
listings.content: Old clubhouse is open to the public for breakfast, lunch, and Sunday brunch. The reason to come here is for the relaxing view of the park and golf course; sit on the porch having a leisurely meal while sipping mimosas or bloody marys.
listings.address: 6500 Magazine St, on Golf Club Drive

listings.name: Tartine
listings.content: French style bakery & cafe; breakfast & lunch. Also has fresh baguettes, scones, etc to go for a tasty picnic in the nearby Audubon Park.

listings.name: The Boot
listings.content: A favorite University District bar for decades. Also has a grill serving bar food and a small convenience store attached.

listings.name: Felipe's
listings.content: Mexican restaurant listed at "eat" above has a nice bar, with frozen margaritas and Mexican beer on tap in addition to standard bar drinks. Unlike most New Orleans bars, not open late.

listings.name: The Palms
listings.content: Bar & grill, mostly University clientele

listings.name: Robert's Bar & Liquor Store
listings.content: Old neighborhood smoky dive bar; pool table and ping-pong table.

listings.name: Park View Guest House
listings.content: Beautiful historic guest house that was built for visitors to the 1884 World's Fair. The side yard is Audubon Park and the streetcar stops right outside, hard to beat the location.

listings.name: St Claude Arts District/SCAD
listings.content: New Orleans newest and hottest arts district that's not your usual tourist-centric arts destination. A true "only in New Orleans" experience. Check website for current exhibits, times, and addresses.

listings.name: The Great War Memorial
listings.content: The first of it kind erected at the end of WWI, this monument pays tribute the fallen residents of the 9th Ward.

listings.name: Vaughan's Lounge
listings.content: Bywater's most famous music venue. Thursday nights when righteous-trumpter/bandleader Kermit Ruffins is in town, he and his BBQ swingers play here; Thursday with Kermit as Vaughan's is a New Orleans favorite. 8:30 PM they say; don't expect shows to start at their clock time in New Orleans, but now that Kermit is a family man, things here tend to start a bit more punctually than they did years ago. Expect crowds and good times. Boiled crawfish or shrimp every Friday. Free Food during Saints games. Following glowing attention in David Simon's series Treme, this place has indeed been discovered by the tourists, but the locals and old-timers don't really care and still show up each Thursdays for some dancing and general fun. Thursdays see free steaming pots of red beans and rice all night long.

listings.name: The Spellcaster Lodge
listings.content: Home of the Amazing Mr. Quintron, Miss Pussycat, and the Drum Buddy workshops. Only open a handful of nights in the year, but this is home to some wild bohemian parties and performances, and, as a visitor, you'll really blow the locals' minds for simply knowing of the place. Stop in if you get a chance.

listings.name: Alombrados Oasis
listings.content: This temple of the Ordo Templi Orientis hosts performances of The Gnostic Mass, conducts initiatory ceremonies, seasonal mystery plays, frequent classes on Thelema, Magick, Yoga, Gnosticism, QBL, Hermetic and Rosicrucian Science, and intensive training programs of Scientific Illuminism. The Oasis also hosts occasional art shows featuring local artists. Contact by phone to attend events. .

listings.name: Chazfest
listings.content: Annual one day music festival held the first Wednesday in April, between the Jazz Fest weekends. (The name is a pun on "Jazz Fest" and popular local bandleader "Washboard Chaz".) 10 hours of great local music on 2 outdoor stages.

listings.name: Dr Bob's Art Gallery
listings.content: A small gallery run by local self-taught folk artist, (you'll see examples of his work at local bars, cafes, and restaurants all over town) with eccentric artwork for sale that will immediately conjure New Orleans and the nearby Cajun Country.

listings.name: Country Club
listings.content: Upscale and stylish American cuisine at great prices, with dining in a beautiful old dining room or on the veranda overlooking the pool. It's a great brunch place. Gay and straight friendly private club and pool in rear, where you can sip cocktails in the jacuzzi into the night (note that it becomes clothing optional).

listings.name: Elizabeth's
listings.content: This is a real local favorite, particularly for breakfast/brunch. Creole and southern food dominates the menu, which combines with friendly service and a cute setting to make for a nice meal any time of day, though. If you have a sweet tooth, don't skip the praline bacon!

listings.name: Frady's
listings.content: This is the sort of place you would only know about if you get a local recommendation—it won't be in your guidebook. For the most part, this is simply a corner store, but the po' boys, particularly the oyster po' boy, are some of the best you'll ever eat. The old-timey Bywater feel to the place is an added plus.

listings.name: Jack Dempsey's
listings.content: This is about as divey and old-school New Orleans as a seafood restaurant can possibly be—you can't be much further from the four star contemporary American dining in Uptown and the Quarter. It's so dark inside, you'll hardly be able to see your big plate of heavily fried seafood and delicious mac 'n cheese (the seafood gumbo and po' boys are decent too).

listings.name: The Joint
listings.content: Excellent down home barbecue with a casual, wooden picnic table-style dining room. If you are trying to decide between Bywater BBQ and the Joint, they are both great; it's a matter of preference between the Joint's dryer style and Bywater BBQ's more wet slabs. Aim first for the ribs and the pulled pork, but really everything is great here.

listings.name: Markey's Bar
listings.content: Great pub food in what can only be described as a standard, classic neighborhood bar (with a few microbrews on tap). Big juicy burgers, fresh salads, and the best wings in the neighborhood. Daily specials and crawfish on Fridays (in season).

listings.name: Satsuma's Cafe
listings.content: A rather hip spot to get your yuppie-ish fix of "fair trade" espresso, fresh juices, quiches, salads, sandwiches, etc. The popularity means long waits on weekends, but the high quality does actually merit the wait.

listings.name: Suis Generis
listings.content: Eclectic innovative cuisine in matching decor. Fresh, tasty, and distinctive.

listings.name: Bacchanal
listings.content: Wine shop, offers wine by the glass—and irregularly has visiting chefs prepare gourmet treats. Now offers lunch too.

listings.name: BJ's Lounge
listings.content: Friendly neighborhood dive with a colorful cast of characters. Beer and booze bar-you're not gonna get an apple martini here. Cookoffs and potlucks are fairly frequent, occasional live music. If you are at Vaughan's Lounge, hop on in and get a bit stronger dose of Bywater.

listings.name: Saturn Bar
listings.content: This is a strange old bohemian dive with some of the city's funkiest and most bizarre decor-soaked in neon and covered in old-school sci-fi posters (sadly, the old jukebox that only played Frank Sinatra's Witchcraft regardless of what you picked is defunct). Drink cheap beer, whiskey, or Southern Comfort. Don't expect them to know how to make fancy-pants mixed drinks. Occasional live music. Rumored to be the favorite of Nick Cage.

listings.name: Vaughan's Lounge
listings.content: Famous as a music venue, but when it isn't hopping with live music a nice place to get a drink and a bit to eat. A good place to watch "New Orleans Saints" football games on TV (as long as you're not rooting for whoever they're playing against!)

listings.name: Bar Redux
listings.content: Bar Redux is an off the beaten track hidden at the end of the world in the Bywater area of New Orleans. The bar's slogan says it all, "Come as you are.... Stay as you like". The interior is decorated with personal items of music memorabilia and retro pop culture treasures. The Bar's exterior features a unique art mural by Street Artist, Michael Roman. The vintage 1936 red neon BAR sign invites you in. Inside you will find a seductively lit area dominated by the infamous 100-year-old (Joe Arones Bar) U-shaped bar from Minneapolis, MN. The bar has a partly covered patio that is decorated with architectural salvage and original art. Homemade pub food and creole classics come out of the kitchen till around 1AM.

listings.name: Lookout Inn Bed & Breakfast
listings.content: A very fashionable B&B with modern, trendy decor and a really attractive, small pool in the courtyard. They play up their "hidden" location's appeal to those who want to stay off the beaten path, and for celebrities who appreciate discretion both on the part of the inn and locals around the area.

listings.name: Maison de Macarty
listings.content: Listed on the National Register of Historic Places, this 1860s Victorian home features five rooms in the main house, two private cottages, and private bath facilities.

listings.name: Po-Boy Festival
listings.content: Big one day festival each November; Oak Street and the surrounding area is lined with food vendors, featuring great po-boy sandwiches and other local treats. Also free live bands and other special events.

listings.name: Chill Out Cafe
listings.content: Asian fusion, omelettes, and waffles.

listings.name: Lebanon's Cafe
listings.content: 1506 S. Carrollton. Good Middle Eastern, half a step above Babylon in price

listings.name: Little Tokyo Small Plates & Noodle Bar
listings.content: Good fresh Japanese, variety from light snacks to full meals. (They also have another location in Mid-City.)

listings.name: Live Oak Cafe
listings.content: Homemade breakfast and Po Boys. Often has a pianist or small combo playing live music in the mornings.

listings.name: Louisiana Pizza Kitchen
listings.content: New Orleans style nouveau pizzas.

listings.name: Pepperoni's Cafe
listings.content: Pizza, calzones, pastas, salads, po-boys.

listings.name: Refuel Cafe
listings.content: Breakfast, lunch and brunch. Omelettes, waffles, gourmet sandwiches, coffees and teas. Free Wi-Fi.

listings.name: Riccobono's Panola Street Cafe
listings.content: 3 blocks down from Carrollton Avenue. Tucked away in a residential section of Carrollton distant from the neighborhood's other restaurants and businesses, Riccobono's does a thriving business of locals for breakfast and lunch. Omelettes, sandwiches, and salads are the specialties.

listings.name: Plum Street Sno-Balls
listings.content: Plum at Burdette: a local delicacy during summer, finely shaved ice with your choice of many custom made syrups. A gourmet version of the northern "snow cone". On Plum Street, a pleasant 3 block walk down from Carrollton Avenue, open 2PM-dark during the long New Orleans summer.

listings.name: PJ's
listings.content: Carrollton's favorite for upscale coffees. Their excellent iced coffee is great on a hot day. Wi-Fi. Now a local chain with branches around town; Maple Street was their first location 30 years ago. Open 6AM-10PM daily.

listings.name: Starbucks
listings.content: National chain.

listings.name: Zotz Coffeehouse
listings.content: Bohemian-gothy coffeehouse with a wide variety of snacks of varied quality. Open until 11PM. Rents computer time & internet access in addition to free Wi-Fi. +1 504 861-2224.

listings.name: Boucherie
listings.content: Creative and tasty Southern cooking. It is housed in a cozy Creole cottage, but plans to move around the corner to Carrollton Avenue. Reservations recommended for evenings and weekends.

listings.name: Cowbell
listings.content: At the far upper end of Oak Street half a dozen blocks up from Carrollton Avenue. Tasty grass-fed beef burgers and other casual quality meat dishes.

listings.name: Fresco's
listings.content: Light Mediterranean and pizza. Lunch and dinner, open until 3AM.

listings.name: GB's Patio Bar and Grill
listings.content: Great freshly-ground meat burgers.

listings.name: Jacques Imo's
listings.content: Trendy version of New Orleans food; people tend to either love or hate it.

listings.name: Jamila's
listings.content: Good quality hearty Mediterranean & Tunisian.

listings.name: La Macarena Pupuseria & Latin Cafe
listings.content: Good fresh Central American style food.

listings.name: Maple Street Cafe
listings.content: Upscale foods like filet mignon at a moderate price.

listings.name: One Restaurant and Lounge
listings.content: Great modern Louisiana food.

listings.name: Brigtsen's
listings.content: One of New Orleans' finest. Reservations needed.

listings.name: Mat and Naddie's
listings.content: Fresh local ingredients, eclectic decoration.

listings.name: Carrollton Station
listings.content: At Dublin a block up from Carrollton.

listings.name: Maple Leaf Bar
listings.content: One of the city's greatest neighborhood live music venues (see "Live Music" section above for more) -- hey, it's also a good bar. The main bar is up front; when things are hopping during live music they also open up the back bar. There's a lovely patio and courtyard in back. Relaxed atmosphere when there's no event going on; chill with a drink, or play a game of pool or chess. Poetry readings every Sunday at 2PM.

listings.name: Snake & Jake's Christmas Lounge
listings.content: Dimly lit shanty, which if you would ever see in the daylight while sober, you'd probably never go in, but if you're in the mood for a funky dive, it's just so darn fun around 3 - 4AM when your other favorites are starting to peter out. Fun bartenders; open 9PM 'til the sun comes up most days! On Oak St., a few blocks down from Carrollton Avenue, between Adams & Hillary Streets.

listings.name: Audubon Aquarium of the Americas
listings.content: A fine aquarium at the foot of Canal Street. Take advantage of the combination ticket, which enables access to the Aquarium, the adjoining Entergy IMAX Theatre, and the Audubon Zoo which is uptown (shuttle provided).
listings.image: Aquarium of the Americas in New Orleans 2.JPG

listings.name: Entergy IMAX Theatre
listings.content: Part of the Audubon Aquarium.

listings.name: Audubon Insectarium
listings.content: An attraction opened in 2008 in the historic old Custom House Building on Canal Street. As it's in a Federal building, you'll pass through a metal detector.

listings.name: Confederate Museum
listings.content: Displays from the American Civil War.

listings.name: Lafayette Square
listings.content: The center of what was the "Old American Quarter" in the early 19th century, with the city's neo-classical city hall and a belle epoch courthouse.
listings.address: bound by St. Charles Ave, Camp St, N Maestri St, and S Maestri St

listings.name: Mardi Gras World
listings.content: The colorful floats for many of the parades of New Orleans Mardi Gras are made here. Experience a taste of Mardi Gras any time of year.

listings.name: Caesars Superdome
listings.content: It was built as the Louisiana Superdome, and is home of the NFL's New Orleans Saints. When no games or events are scheduled, you can take tours.

listings.name: Smoothie King Center
listings.content: Located beside the Superdome, the Smoothie King Center (formerly New Orleans Arena) hosts smaller shows & sporting events. Most notably home to the NBA's New Orleans Pelicans.

listings.name: Morial Convention Center
listings.content: The first part of the city's large convention center complex was built during the 1984 World's Fair and is named after a former mayor.
listings.image: FEMA - 37154 - Louisiana Convention Center in New Orleans Ernest N. Morial.jpg

listings.name: National World War II Museum
listings.content: Formerly the "D-Day Museum". Exhibits on the United States in World War II on the battlefronts and the home front. It has a restaurant, the "Victory Theater" presenting multi-media historical presentation, and the "Stage Door Canteen" featuring live music shows in the style of World War II-era USO shows.
listings.image: Main entrance to the National World War II Museum.jpg

listings.name: Ogden Museum of Southern Art
listings.image: Howard Library Camp Higgins Museums NOLA Nov 2011.JPG

listings.name: Caesars New Orleans
listings.content: The state's only land-based casino (there are riverboat gambling venues in the suburbs).

listings.name: Howlin' Wolf
listings.content: They host a good variety of local and visiting acts; definitely get a hold of their schedule in The Gambit, a weekly paper. (If you visited here before Katrina, they are now a block up the street from their former location.)

listings.name: Mulate's
listings.content: At Convention Center Boulevard. Cajun music.

listings.name: Orpheum Theatre
listings.content: Home of the Louisiana Philharmonic Orchestra.

listings.name: Saenger Theater
listings.content: At Canal Street. The most gorgeous of the city's beautiful old picture palace theaters.

listings.name: Le Salon
listings.content: Swanky hotel bar often has good jazz pianists, vocalists, and small combos.

listings.name: Cafe Du Monde
listings.content: Sells chicory-flavored coffee with New Orleans beignets.

listings.name: City Greens
listings.content: Soups, salad, wraps; breakfast & lunch.

listings.name: La Boca
listings.content: Argentine steak house.

listings.name: Merchant
listings.content: Crepes, quiches, sandwiches, salads.

listings.name: Mulate's
listings.content: At Convention Center Boulevard. The other well known Cajun place.

listings.name: Emeril's
listings.content: In the Warehouse District.

listings.name: Grill Room at Windsor Court Hotel
listings.content: Contender for best restaurant, but very expensive; in the CBD just down from the Casino. They also serve a fine high-tea.

listings.name: Palace Cafe
listings.content: French Creole, noted for the seafood and duck dishes, and the luscious white chocolate bread pudding.

listings.name: Restaurant August
listings.content: Renowned chef John Besh's signature restaurant featuring Contemporary French with a focus on local ingredients. Menu balances seafood, fowl and meat. Try either the 5 course tasting or the John Besh "Degustation" menu which changes nightly.

listings.name: Gordon Biersch
listings.content: Handcrafted beer brewery and restaurant.

listings.name: Lucy's Retired Surfer Bar
listings.content: Relaxed. All-you-can-eat crawfish party Sunday evenings.

listings.name: Sazerac Bar
listings.content: In the Roosevelt Hotel. Sip signature drinks like the original Sazerac cocktail or the Ramos gin fiz.

listings.name: Whiskey Blue
listings.content: Swank upscale bar

listings.name: Hostelling International
listings.content: This hostel offers both shared dorms and ensuite private rooms. Bathrooms for dorm guests are in the hallway, but they are all single-use. Dorms also have security lockers. Free breakfast and free wireless internet available.

listings.name: Les Carillons
listings.content: Towards the upper end of the CBD, close to the Julia Street art galleries.

listings.name: Embassy Suites New Orleans - Convention Center
Hilton New Orleans Riverside
listings.content: 3-star Hilton on the banks of the Mississippi River, in storied New Orleans, Louisiana adjacent to the Ernest N. Morial Convention Center and only three blocks from the French Quarter.

listings.name: Courtyard New Orleans Downtown/Convention Center
listings.content: Two blocks from Morial Convention Center.

listings.name: Hyatt Place New Orleans Convention Center
listings.content: Across the street from the New Orleans Convention Center. It offers upscale lodging.

listings.name: Hyatt Regency New Orleans
listings.content: Near the Superdome and City Hall.

listings.name: InterContinental New Orleans
listings.content: Luxury hotel on the St. Charles Mardi Gras parade route.

listings.name: International House Hotel
listings.content: Boutique hotel 2 blocks from the French Quarter.

listings.name: Le Pavillon
listings.content: One of the fanciest hotels in the city with the exception of the Ritz Carlton and Windsor Court. Elegant French and Old South stylings in the lobby. Featuring a Sunday "Jazz Brunch" with live music as well as a rooftop jacuzzi.

listings.name: Loft 523
listings.content: Boutique hotel 2 blocks from the French Quarter.

listings.name: Ritz-Carlton
listings.content: Top notch hotel in what had been the Maison Blanche Department Store building. It's the Windsor Court's rival for finest in town.

listings.name: The Roosevelt
listings.content: One of the city's grand old hotels; reopened in 2009 after a $145-million restoration modernized the rooms, returned the lobby to its historic glory, and reopened the famous Sazerac Bar and the Blue Room dinner & music venue. The lobby is worth a look even if you're not staying here.

listings.name: The Whitney
listings.content: A New Orleans hotel registered as a historic landmark.

listings.name: Windsor Court Hotel
listings.content: One of the finer hotels in town, If you want the tops and are willing to pay top dollar for it, this is the place.

listings.name: Ashé Cultural Center
listings.content: Ashé's mission, essentially, is to be a community gathering space for the creation of art, but also to help drive community renewal. You'll need to check the website, but they have occasional events that would appeal to a visitor, like drum workshops, film screenings, etc.

listings.name: Lafayette Cemetery #2
listings.content: Unlike the interesting Lafayette Cemetery #1, #2 has not been maintained and is not terribly safe anyway. The same can be said for adjacent St. Joseph Cemetery #1. New Orleans has many more interesting and safer cemeteries; skip these.

listings.name: Southern Food and Beverage Museum
listings.content: Museum founded in 2004 about the food of the southern US.

listings.name: Hotel Hope
listings.content: This homeless shelter for women and children used to be the Crescent Palms Motel, which originally opened as Mason's Hotel, a black-owned hotel where black guests would be welcomed. As such, it attracted and hosted not a few African American celebrities, like Mary Wells, The Drifters, the Marvelettes and Martha and the Vandellas. You can appreciate it from the outside even though the neighborhood is a bit rough, or maybe drop in and make a donation.

listings.name: Cafe Reconcile
listings.content: Reconcile is one part tasty Creole restaurant and one part social work—the mission is to train 16-22 year-olds from the neighborhood for a career in the restaurant industry, by giving them experience and instruction for serving and line cooking. So you'll be eating well and feeling good about where your money is going. The interior is a really nice bright place to hang out too. For dessert, you must try their award-winning Bananas Foster Bread Pudding.

listings.name: Cajun Seafood
listings.content: This is a great takeout for seafood boil (crab, shrimp, and especially the spicy crawfish), but it also has good po' boys, wings, and MSG-laden Chinese food for good measure. In other words, this place is take out for a party in your hotel room just waiting to happen.

listings.name: Philly's Cafe
listings.content: Solid Philly cheesesteaks in a town where a good cheesesteak is hard to come by.

listings.name: Heard Dat Kitchen
listings.content: New Orleans' most dangerous BBQ. It's quite good, but the neighborhood is rough. Even the inside looks like it might cut you if you look at it the wrong way. If you have any fear of the city, this place is not for you. If on the other hand, you will brave the mean streets for some mean meats, by all means, stop by and grab some ribs. "BYOB".

listings.name: Fort Pike State Historic Site
listings.content: While it lies within the city limits, the fort is some 20 miles away from the urban area, on Highway 90 towards Slidell, at "the Rigolets", a water pass into Lake Pontchartrain. Interesting, well-preserved old fort built in the 1820s, saw some minor action during the American Civil War. Visitable by appointment only, to be scheduled (at least two weeks in advance) between the hours of 9AM-5PM.

listings.name: Lakefront Airport
listings.content: This was the city's airport back before the arrival of the big jets and the new New Orleans International airport was built out in Kenner. Lakefront Airport still keeps busy with private and company planes. The 1930s vintage main terminal building and the nearby sculpture fountain by Enrique Alfarez are treats for lovers of Art Deco. The terminal's main facade was freshly restored in 2010; restoration work on the interior is ongoing.

listings.name: NASA Michoud
listings.content: This was the site of the village of Michoud before it was absorbed into New Orleans, then a World War II Defense plant that made landing craft and aircraft, and since 1961 a NASA facility. Apollo Moon Rocket boosters were built here, and in recent decades, the fuel tanks for the Space Shuttle. With the end of the Shuttle program, the future for NASA Michoud is uncertain. Meanwhile, visitors can park briefly in the little visitor lot on Old Gentilly Road, to look or take a snapshot of an Apollo Saturn V booster on display out front, a pair of smokestacks from the antebellum Michoud Plantation preserved in front of the main building, and what you can see of the outside of the Assembly Building from this spot. (Visitors are not allowed inside without advance arrangement and a sponsor, although on rare occasions limited numbers of the public are allowed in to part of the facility for special events.)

listings.name: Ba Mien Restaurant
listings.content: Vietnamese. While often overshadowed by the ravings inspired by Dong Phuong, this is still a great option, with a nicer atmosphere inside—brighter, more spacious, etc. The minty house specials are in particular worth seeking out.

listings.name: Castnet Seafood
listings.content: When you go to New Orleans, and you find a shack that says "seafood" on the side, and it has enough people packed into and snaking out the front door to alarm a fire marshall, you better come to the party hungry. The crawfish, shrimp, and crab boils are excellent, as are the profoundly over-stuffed po' boys (if it's in season, they do a soft shell crab po' boy). Bottom line is that if you like seafood fresh, fried, or boiled, you should go way out of your way to find this place—if you are claustrophobic, bring someone else with you to go inside and order. Picnic tables out back.

listings.name: Deanie's
listings.content: Another great bet out east for local seafood, fried or fresh, along with some other New Orleans standards. Deanie's on Hayne is not to be confused with the Deanie's in the French Quarter. Unsurprisingly, those bacon-wrapped shrimp taste really good.

listings.name: Dong Phuong Restaurant
listings.content: Perhaps Little Vietnam's most esteemed restaurant serves a variety of Vietnamese dishes, and also has a bakery and sandwich shop and bubble teas. The sit down restaurant is on the right side of the building, the bakery & sandwiches to go on the right. Make a point to grab a loaf of French bread on your way out—while startling, it's perhaps not unintuitive that a bakery from the former French colony of Vietnam is producing some of the best French bread in New Orleans.

listings.name: Vucinovich's Restaurant
listings.content: Run by a big Italian family with a Slavic last name, this place serves some of the best fried seafood and chicken that you will find in the city. They also do various Creole dishes, some great po' boys, and a few Italian entrées, but the fried foods is where it's at. If the location on Michoud didn't give it away, they do their business with the lunch crowd from the NASA Michoud Assembly Facility down the road—hence the limited hours.

listings.name: Walker's Southern Style BBQ
listings.content: Attached to Castnet Seafood is this mysterious, nearly never open BBQ hole in the wall has brilliant cue on offer: brisket, ribs, pulled pork, links, smoked chicken, etc., plus great sides. But all this pales in comparison to their highly acclaimed cochon de lait po' boy (Esquire included it in its "Top 30 Sandwiches in America" list). Cochon de lait is, strictly speaking, a whole suckling pig slow-roasted over hardwood, and a cause for a backwoods Cajun party throughout the roasting process. Walker's cochon de lait is actually done with pork butts, slow roasted on a rotisserie over hardwood, before making its way to one heck of a po' boy. They have served their po' boys for years at the Jazz and Heritage Festival to rapt audiences, but you can actually get them year round at this little storefront, but call ahead to place an order—the waits during their tiny open hours are long, and there is always the possibility that this little operation will be closed on a given day.

listings.name: Nha Trang
listings.content: Karaoke bar and restaurant.

listings.name: Riverboat Travel Park
listings.content: An RV park that is reasonably close to the French Quarter without, ahem, being right next to the Iberville Housing Projects.

listings.name: Super 8
listings.content: This is by far the best consumer-rated property in Eastern New Orleans, with an attentive staff. The building is even a little stylish, with a balcony-laden old New Orleans style to it, plus courtyard pool. You are in the middle of nowhere, of course, but the hotel does offer rare free parking, and is a dependable budget chain option.

listings.name: Holiday Inn Express New Orleans East
listings.content: They have an outdoor pool and those little cheese omelettes that make you question the origin.

listings.name: Country Inn & Suites by Radisson
listings.content: Real omelettes on the breakfast bar here.

listings.name: Cafe Istanbul
listings.content: Named after a legendary Frenchmen Street venue of a generation ago, the new Cafe Istanbul is theater space with a bar in the New Orleans Healing Center, a renovated old warehouse building now a community center. Live theater, music, dance, film, and other performances.

listings.name: 13 Monaghan
listings.content: An Irish themed bar and grill, squeezed into an odd warehouse space. Good Irish beers and late-night grub, including Huevos Rancheros and pulled pork sandwich. Vegan options available.

listings.name: Cafe Rose Nicaud
listings.content: Coffees, teas, and fresh deli sandwiches, quiches.

listings.name: Cake Cafe
listings.content: Great bakery with sandwiches.

listings.name: Flora Gallery and Coffee Shop
listings.content: Ultra-funky coffeehouse with light fare, as well as poetry readings, board games, and the like.

listings.name: Mona's
listings.content: Middle Eastern cuisine, with excellent shwarmas, and an extensive vegetarian selection. Other locations around the city.

listings.name: Schiro's Community Cafe & Bar
listings.content: Great food, reasonably priced. Great vegan/vegetarian selections, even for breakfast. Small community market attached.

listings.name: WhoDat Coffee
listings.content: Friendly coffee shop with free wireless internet and easy parking. Gourmet coffee and tea, soup, salad, sandwich and pastry selection, reasonably priced.

listings.name: Breakaway's R & B
listings.content: Your Favorite Creole Cookhouse in The Marigny.New Orleans Unofficial Rock & Roll Hall of FameFrom the Chef of Green Goddess. The name is inspired by Irma Thomas’ song “Breakaway.” The R&B means restaurant and bar more than rhythm and blues, but the Artigues liked the idea of a reference to local music to help set the tone for their neighborhood place.

listings.name: Alois J. Binder Bakery
listings.content: Breads and pastries to go.

listings.name: The Orange Couch
listings.content: Coffee house with light snacks, ice cream, and WiFi.

listings.name: Adolfo's
listings.content: Cozy, slightly quirky yet charming Italian. Let the waiters guide you to the nightly specials.

listings.name: Feelings Cafe
listings.content: The way the French Quarter used to be 50 years ago. Great piano bar, balcony overlooking nice courtyard. Definitely a locals place and great value, but not for the homophobic.

listings.name: Marigny Brasserie
listings.content: Good menu, and a popular wine and martini bar.

listings.name: Praline Connection
listings.content: Much more than pralines (a sweet pecan candy), good Creole soul food at a reasonable price.

listings.name: Sukho Thai
listings.content: Authentic Thai food in a neighborhood cafe.

listings.name: Wasabi
listings.content: Excellent sushi and Japanese cuisine. Good selection of sakes.

listings.name: Apple Barrel
listings.content: Sometimes has live music too. Local characters, low prices, no attitude.

listings.name: AllWays
listings.content: Lounge in the front, small theater in the back. The hub of fringe theater, plays, bands, and variety shows often. Very friendly and comfortable for all.

listings.name: d.b.a.
listings.content: New York style bar on Frenchmen, if you need a bit of sophistication when you drink. Great selection of beers, and frequent live music.

listings.name: Dragon's Den
listings.content: A charmingly dilapidated, well-hidden club (go down the building's side alley, then up the stairs to your left), with a balcony on Esplanade and an opium-den feel inside. Live music, occasional poetry slams, serves food.

listings.name: Friendly Bar
listings.content: Gay neighborhood bar where locals gather to hang out in a no-pressure atmosphere.

listings.name: Iggy's
listings.content: Neighborhood bar with a lot of neighborhood characters; very friendly for all. Frequently serves food.

listings.name: The John
listings.content: Relaxed neighborhood hangout with rockabilly, country, and punk on the jukebox. Named for the gold-painted toilet seats that serve as stools at the tables. With inexpensive stiff drinks served up in Mason jars, this spot for locals offers one of the best deals on Frenchmen St.

listings.name: Mimi's in the Marigny
listings.content: The toniest bar in the Marigny (but hardly pretentious), with billiards, Galaga, occasional live music, and tapas served from the restaurant upstairs. Good selection of beers and specialty drinks. Hip Hop and Funk DJs Friday and Saturday nights. Lots of singles on the weekends.

listings.name: Phoenix
listings.content: Gay neighborhood bar by day, catering to the leather crowd at night. Also the official United Cab stand for catching rides back into the French Quarter.

listings.name: R-Bar
listings.content: Hip but laid-back hangout that's comfortable by day and happening at night; great jukebox.

listings.name: Blue Nile
listings.content: A staple of the Frenchmen Street set of music venues, Blue Nile serves up funk, blues, jazz, and New Orleans-style brass bands. A plus is the big dance floor. Unlike most places in Marigny, though, it often charges a cover, so be sure to sample the music from outside before making the decision to go in.

listings.name: Buffa's Lounge
listings.content: Small bar room in the front; the big room in the back (also accessible from the side door on Burgundy Street) hosts live music and other events, including a popular jazz brunch on Sundays.

listings.name: Checkpoint Charlies
listings.content: This bar has bands, pool tables and laundry facilities if your clothes need awashin'. Local rock and jump bands.

listings.name: The Maison
listings.content: The place to go for dinner + jazz (pretty energetic jazz), with the largest dining room on the street, and three stages for music.

listings.name: Snug Harbor
listings.content: Perhaps the city's foremost modern jazz venue.

listings.name: The Spotted Cat Music Club
listings.content: Cozy bar with good hot jazz.

listings.name: Aaron Ingram Haus
listings.content: One and two bedroom suites six blocks from Bourbon Street.

listings.name: Auld Sweet Olive Bed and Breakfast
listings.content: Historic home with six rooms, each with private bath. Hand painted wall treatments, attractive gardens.

listings.name: B&W Courtyards
listings.content: Three 19th century buildings connected by lush courtyards. Private baths. Architectural award winner.

listings.name: 1870 Banana Courtyard B&B
listings.content: In 1800s former elite bordello. B&B now. Balcony rooms with a view or budget rooms, each w/different theme. Lagniappe: free soft drinks, bottled water, generous continental breakfast. Tropical courtyard with hammock, verandah with porch swing. Wi-Fi. New fangled stuff, ensuite like: private bathrooms, cable TV, phone, heat and A/C. Gated parking lot.

listings.name: The Burgundy Bed and Breakfast
listings.content: Gay owned and operated, affordable rates.

listings.name: Chez Nous Guest House
listings.content: One and two bedroom private suites.

listings.name: The Claiborne Mansion
listings.content: An outstanding 19th century mansion and a wonderful hostess, Cleo. .

listings.name: Creole Inn
listings.content: A cozy and affordable B&B.

listings.name: Crescent City Guest House
listings.content: 4 Guest rooms each with private bathrooms. All taxes, maid service and continental breakfast included. Free off-street parking and WiFi.

listings.name: Elysian Fields Inn
listings.content: Hosts, Leigh and Jim are very knowledgeable of the NOLA music scene. Has secure covered parking.

listings.name: La Dauphine, Residence des Artistes
listings.content: A Bohemian, laid-back, unpretentious, 2 room 1896 guest house for the budget-minded traveler- with a 3-night minimum; private baths, free Internet. Advance reservations required. Ray & Kim are the warm and friendly hosts.

listings.name: La Maison Marigny Bed and Breakfast
listings.content: One of Travel & Leisure Magazine's TOP TEN B&Bs.

listings.name: Maison DuBois Bed and Breakfast
listings.content: Bed and breakfast.

listings.name: Marigny Manor House
listings.content: 1840s Grand Greek Revival home.

listings.name: Old Town Inn
listings.content: Cool historic inn, three separate buildings, dating from the 1800s.

listings.name: Pierre Coulon Guest House
listings.content: Comfortable small apartment.

listings.name: River House
listings.content: A lovingly-restored antebellum mansion with three unique apartments, each like no other.

listings.name: Royal Street Inn B&B
listings.content: "B&B" here may stand for "Bed and Beverage", as this is upstairs from the R-Bar.

listings.name: Suite Jazz
listings.content: Circa 1861, the building has typical high ceilings, chandeliers, hardwood floors, Cable TV, WIFI Internet Access, Central Air, a fully stocked kitchen and more! A queen sleigh bed, travertine tiled shower & original artwork by fabulous artists. Windows have added sound protection. Sylvia is one of New Orleans' best ambassadors and a great concierge/hostess/tour guide.

listings.name: Sunburst Inn
listings.content: Historic Victorian house with one and two bedroom suites with private bath. A short walk to French Quarter. Suites has lots of nice amenities, located in quite charming neighborhood.

listings.name: Lions Inn Bed and Breakfast
listings.content: Features ten non-smoking guest rooms. Most have private baths while some share a bath. All have twin, king, and queen-sized beds. Among its most appealing features is a garden with swimming pool and Jacuzzi hot tub.

listings.name: River House New Orleans
listings.content: Three-story antebellum guest house with separate apartments on each floor. Amenities include complementary Wi-Fi and a swimming pool. Rates are lower during the summer (June 1-August 31) and higher during special events (Mardi Gras, French Quarter Fest, New Orleans Jazz & Heritage Festival, Halloween, and New Years Eve). All payments must go through Airbnb or VRBO. A 2-night minimum stay is required.

listings.name: Bourbon Street
listings.content: Some 8 blocks of Bourbon from Canal Street down are given over to catering to the hard drinking tourists. If getting drunk with other tourists is the goal of your vacation, this is the place for you. Even otherwise, this notorious strip of tourist traps is worth at least a quick look for its gaudy sleaziness. Bourbon has not only countless bars but also many fine restaurants featuring delicious local cuisine for people who want to experience the local foods.

listings.name: Royal Street
listings.content: Strolling Royal Street by day is as essential a New Orleans experience as Bourbon Street by night. 1 block away in distance, a world in attitude. There are art galleries, upscale antique stores, landmark hotels and interesting specialty shops. Lots of temptations for those with money, but is also fun window shopping for those not spending a dime.

listings.name: Jackson Square
listings.content: The old town square, often live music is going on here, as well as street corner painters and tarot readers. Around the square are:.

listings.name: Cabildo
listings.content: Colonial city hall, now a museum; Louisiana Purchase agreements transferring the city from France to the USA were signed here.
listings.price: $10 adults, $8 students/seniors/military, free for children 6 and under

listings.name: Presbytere
listings.content: Colonial church offices, now another museum, including exhibits on New Orleans Mardi Gras and the city's recovery from Hurricane Katrina.
listings.price: $7 adults, $6 students/seniors/military, free for children 6 and under

listings.name: St. Louis Cathedral
listings.content: A symbol of New Orleans, this is the oldest Roman Catholic Cathedral in the United States and has a giant statue of the Virgin Mary with her arms extended gracing the middle of the courtyard.

listings.name: Pontalba Buildings
listings.content: 4-story brick apartment buildings have specialty shops, restaurants, and a tourist information office on the ground floors.

listings.name: Moon Walk
listings.content: A brick walking path along the Mississippi River across Decatur Street from Jackson Square. The curious name comes from its dedication to former New Orleans mayor Moon Landrieu.

listings.name: Chartres Street
listings.content: Parallels Bourbon and Royal Streets, one block closer to the river than Royal. While less famous with visitors, those who enjoy historic architecture will find the city's greatest concentration of preserved colonial era buildings along Chartres, along with early 19th century town-houses. Plus it passes through Jackson Square. A pleasant walk with local shops, cafes, restaurants, and bars scattered along the street.

listings.name: Old French Market
listings.content: While souvenirs for visitors have taken over a good bit of the space at this more than 250-year-old market, there are still vendors selling fresh produce as in days of old. On weekends a much larger number of vendors set up here, with handicrafts and flea market type goods.
listings.address: bound by Ursulines Ave, N Peters St, Barracks St, and French Market Pl

listings.name: Lower Decatur Street
listings.content: Right around the corner from the historic US Mint, and the French Market. A French Quarter neighborhood with shops, dining, and entertainment. Late at night the bars really hop with local color.

listings.name: New Orleans Jazz Park Visitor's Center & Headquarters
listings.content: Often has live music, lectures, and gives music history related walking tours. Many events are free; those that aren't are a bargain.

listings.name: Jean Lafitte National Park and Preserve
listings.content: Headquarters for National Park that includes several historic sites in and near New Orleans. Has a small museum and visitor's center. Show up by 9AM to get a place on the informative free walking tour of the French Quarter.

listings.name: Historic New Orleans Collection
listings.content: Museum with changing exhibits of local history. Also has a research center nearby on Chartres Street.

listings.name: Old U.S. Mint
listings.content: Coins haven't been minted in New Orleans for decades, so the building is now a museum, with the minting process downstairs and the world's top exhibit on New Orleans jazz upstairs.
listings.price: $6 adults, $5 students/seniors/military, free for children 12 and under

listings.name: Old Ursuline Convent
listings.content: Completed in 1752, open for tours.
listings.price: $5 adults, $4 seniors, $3 students, free for children under 6

listings.name: Pharmacy Museum
listings.content: See and learn about medical practices of the mid 19th century. Calling ahead to verify hours is recommended. Reservations required for guided tours.
listings.price: Guided Tours: Adult $15, Senior/Student/Military $10; Self-Guided: Adults $10, Senior/Student/Military $7. Children 6 and under: Free

listings.name: Cigar Factory New Orleans & Museum
listings.content: History and tradition of one of New Orleans' oldest traditions -- cigar rolling! Watch the masters at work daily in the only operating cigar factory since the 1950s.

listings.name: Musee Conti Wax Museum
listings.content: Experience more than 300 years of history, legend and scandal with the 154 life-size figures displayed in historically accurate settings.

listings.name: 1850 House
listings.price: $3 adults, $2 students/seniors/military, free for children 12 and under

listings.name: Beauregard-Keyes House
listings.price: $10 adults, $9 students/seniors, $4 children 6-12, free for children under 6

listings.name: Hermann-Grima House
listings.content: 1830s mansion.
listings.price: $10 adults, $8 students/seniors/children 8-18/AAA members, free for children under 8. Joint admission with the Gallier House $18 adults, $15 students/seniors/children 8-18/AAA members

listings.name: Gallier House
listings.content: Home of famous local 19th-century architect.
listings.price: $10 adults, $8 students/seniors/children 8-18/AAA members, free for children under 8. Joint admission with the Hermann-Grima House $18 adults, $15 students/seniors/children 8-18/AAA members

listings.name: Madame John's Legacy
listings.content: 18th-century Creole home.

listings.name: Carriage rides
listings.content: Mule-drawn carriages have driven tourists around the Quarter since the gasoline rationing of the 1940s. Carriage drivers are licensed tour guides and give tourists a full blown tour consisting of a mix of history, architecture, restaurants & stories, though some drivers have been known to spin stories that are more colorful than factual. Available to tourists is a 30-minute tour of the French Quarter, hour tour of the St. Louis No.1 Cemetery/French Quarter combo, hour and one half or two hour Garden District tour, or any combination thereof. Carriage drivers also do bar-hopping tours, shopping by carriage, Marigny tours & ghost tours. There are several options from group rates 6-8 people to private tours for 1-4 people. Things have changed quite a bit in the carriage industry in the past 7 years! Drivers are more customer service oriented & courteous.

listings.name: Street entertainers
listings.content: Performing for tips from tourists, varying greatly in talent. The still mime-ers are a sight to see, they stand still alone or with a partner and when you give them a tip they will move very slowly in tandem, like a robot. There are excellent musicians who enjoy keeping up their chops out of doors. There are also hacks with little talent other than scamming money. Beware of the Got-yo-shoes-ers; these are scammers who go up to tourists saying "I bet you I know whe' you got yo' shoes!". If they succeed in getting the tourist to take the bet, the answer is "You got yo' shoes on yo' feet!" They usually have a large and threatening-looking friend or someone who looks like they just smoked too much crack nearby to make sure bets are paid. You will almost always encounter one of these burnt out hustlers, when they do just politely reply: "They are on my feet" and they will know the jig is up.

listings.name: Walking tours
listings.content: Plentiful but often pricey. Most cost $10-20 per person, but there are a couple of good, free walking tours. Or you can simply walk and see all of the landmarks since most are labeled and you can go in and read about it yourself. Park rangers from the Jean Lafitte National Park (see above) offer a free walking tour of the French Quarter that is very informative. Space is very limited, and spots on the tour are only given out on the day of the tour at 9AM. You should try to show up at least half an hour early to reserve a spot. You'll learn the real history of New Orleans, which is often as colorful as the tall stories.

listings.name: Aquarium of the Americas
listings.content: The only aquarium in New Orleans. In the French Quarter. Features an IMAX theatre. 10AM-5PM daily.
listings.image: Aquarium of the Americas, New Orleans, after Katrina.jpg

listings.name: Audubon Insectarium
listings.content: In the historic Old Customs House Building. The Audubon Institute, which also runs the nearby Aquarium and the Zoo up in the Audubon District, opened the Insectarium in 2008. 10a-5p daily.

listings.name: Fritzels
listings.content: Good house bands in the evenings, and is often a venue for out-of-town and international musicians versed in the New Orleans style.

listings.name: Maison Bourbon
listings.content: Sometimes has decent bands (though as often doesn't), as many good local Dixieland players lacking a better gig for the moment often wind up here. As the doors are open to the street, you can listen a bit from outside, judge for yourself whether they have a band you'd enjoy, and walk on by or go on in as appropriate.

listings.name: New Orleans Jazz Park
listings.content: Actually in "Dutch Alley", the French Market pedestrian alley on the river side of Decatur between Dumaine and St. Philip Streets. Often has free live music weekend afternoons and sometimes other times.
listings.price: Free, some park programs have a fee

listings.name: Palm Court Jazz Cafe
listings.content: Those who prefer their old style New Orleans jazz in a somewhat more upscale atmosphere where dinner and drinks are served should be sure to visit this place in the lower Quarter. Some of the same musicians who play Preservation Hall play here on other nights, along with other top local classic style jazz greats. The owner's husband runs the Jazzology record company, featuring the world's largest independent label catalogue of trad jazz, so you can pick up CDs by your favorites from Bunk Johnson to current Dixielanders while you're here.

listings.name: Preservation Hall
listings.content: Established in 1961 to preserve Traditional New Orleans jazz. Talk about atmosphere! Listen to real jazz and nothing else (no booze, no bathrooms). You'll have to stand in line, and most people will stand through the set (accommodations will be made for those who can't stand that long; call +1 504-522-2841, or email info@preservationhall.com in advance). Sets each night from 5PM, Sa and Su from 2:30PM. Arrive at least 15 minutes before the set starts.
listings.price: 45-minute set: front row $50, seated $40, standing room $25 for advance online purchase seats (cash purchase at the door is no longer available)

listings.name: Acme Oyster House
listings.content: No ambiance, but good oysters and other southern delights. Be ready to wait in line. Great food, Great price. 1/2 dozen chargrilled oysters for $9.99 simply can't be beat, especially since Louisiana oysters are far superior in size to those from anyplace else. For an entertaining and social experience, sit at the bar, where you can talk to the oyster shuckers about the celebrities and pro athletes who have visited in the restaurant.

listings.name: Bennachin
listings.content: African food. Good lunch specials. Many vegetarian and vegan options.

listings.name: Cafe Envie
listings.content: Sandwiches, salads, omelets, quiches. Wireless internet access.

listings.name: Central Grocery
listings.content: Old Italian-American grocery sandwich shop, famous for their enormous muffuletta sandwiches originated by this family in 1910. One is enough to feed four hungry people! Order 1/2 to start for 2 people!

listings.name: Clover Grill
listings.content: Good eggs, burgers, and such. Heavily (though not exclusively) gay clientele. They cook your burger under a hubcap!

listings.name: Coop's Place
listings.content: You can get good Cajun food at a really good price here. Locals favorite. Best fried chicken in the city! Patrons must be 21 or older to enter due to the presence of video poker machines.

listings.name: Felix's Restaurant & Oyster Bar
listings.content: The Acme's traditional competition and usually a shorter wait, too. A very good oyster bar with other traditional Cajun fare.

listings.name: Jimani
listings.content: When you want a great roast beef sandwich at 2AM.

listings.name: Johnny's Po-Boys
listings.content: Lunch counter with some eat-in tables; one of the largest po-boy menus around. Excellent breakfast biscuit sandwich!

listings.name: Mona Lisa's
listings.content: Italian and pizza.

listings.name: Port of Call
listings.content: Awesome, huge burgers and loaded baked potatoes. Potent drinks, parrot-head juke box. Lil slice of paradise.

listings.name: Yo Mama's Bar and Grill
listings.content: Limited but high quality grill menu, including 14 types of burgers.

listings.name: Rampart Treehouse
listings.content: Pizza Slice Bar that serves a rich pizza menu, art, cocktails, and beer. Our space is covered from floor to ceiling in artwork that is from artists from around the globe.

listings.name: Cafe du Monde
listings.content: Serves coffee and beignets. The cafe has been a local landmark since the 19th century and is across the street from St Ann St, which faces Jackson Square. Before the COVID-19 pandemic, the cafe was open 24 hours daily. It often attracted long lines and crowds of locals and tourists during both the day and night. After a temporary shutdown at the beginning of the pandemic, the cafe has since reopened.

listings.name: CC's Coffee House
listings.content: The lower French Quarter branch of a small local chain. Great iced coffee drinks for hot days.

listings.name: Croissant d'Or
listings.content: French pastries and light breakfasts & lunch.

listings.name: Bayona
listings.content: Incredible French/Euro/NOLA food by esteemed chef, Susan Spicer. Fabulous wine selections. Many locals' favorite. Must RSVP.

listings.name: French Market Restaurant and Bar
listings.content: Serves boiled crawfish and other down-home delicacies. Happy hour M-F 3-5PM with raw oysters $.50 each. Has downstairs restaurant and balcony seating upstairs.

listings.name: El Gato Negro
listings.content: A local favorite for Mexican. Breakfast available on the weekends.

listings.name: Green Goddess
listings.content: Small restaurant tucked away on a side street serving creative dishes. Opened in 2009 and quickly became a favorite with local foodies. A few years later it's certainly been "discovered"; try to go there sometime other than the busiest days and not during the busiest dinner hours to avoid long waits for a table.

listings.name: Gumbo Shop
listings.content: An institution for gumbos and similar traditional Louisiana dishes.

listings.name: Italian Barrel
listings.content: Northern Italian cuisine with an Italian-focused wine list. The outdoor tables are across from the New Orleans Jazz Museum’s outdoor stage, and Frenchmen Street’s live-music venues are nearby. Reservations are recommended during peak dinner hours.

listings.name: Louisiana Pizza Kitchen
listings.content: Upscale pizzeria in the French Market.

listings.name: Mr. B's Bistro
listings.content: Storied, elegant restaurant whose signature dish is the (non-grilled) BBQ shrimp.

listings.name: Remoulade
listings.content: A casual spin-off of Arnaud's where you can try their famous Caesar salad dressing and the eponymous remoulade without wearing a jacket and tie. Same shrimp remoulade and gumbo as the main restaurant for a lower price.

listings.name: Sylvain
listings.content: Opened in 2010; quality food and drink in a beautiful Spanish Colonial era building.

listings.name: Tujague's
listings.content: Pronounced "two jacks"; despite the weird spelling, it's been here since 1856 so they must be doing something right. The locals swear by it.

listings.name: Antoine's
listings.content: Antoine's lays claim to being the oldest same family owned restaurant in the country. Opening in 1840, this French Creole restaurant is where Oysters Rockefeller was invented in the 1890s -- and the only restaurant where the original authentic Oysters Rockefeller can be eaten, as the recipe is a closely guarded secret. Your waiter is your guide here; treat them well and ask their recommendations. Before dining, ask your server for a tour of the historic restaurant. There are more than 15 dining rooms, all of which reek of tradition and are steeped in history. Make sure to take a peek down the vast and cavernous wine cellar, which can take the breath away from a true wine lover. Antoine's has opened a beautiful new bar. Step off of St. Louis and step into history.

listings.name: Arnaud's
listings.content: Another of the great old French Quarter classics.

listings.name: Brennan's
listings.content: One of the famous local traditions; fine Creole cuisine, known for their gourmet breakfasts. Ask to sit in the courtyard, on the balcony, or in one of the upstairs rooms. Be sure to try the Bananas Foster, which was invented here. Great for upscale New Orleans breakfast.

listings.name: Court of Two Sisters
listings.content: A place for daily brunch (with a live jazz combo) and post-night out hangover cures; beautiful courtyard.

listings.name: Galatoire's
listings.content: Classic Creole on Bourbon Street. Despite being in the tourist strip of Bourbon Street, locals do eat here. For the true experience, wait in line for the downstairs dining room (reservations can be made for the upstairs room, but locals don't eat there), and refuse the menu when you're seated. Let your waiter know your tastes and let him feed you.

listings.name: NOLA
listings.content: Very good, run by chef Emeril Lagasse, not quite as pricey as his namesake restaurant in the Central Business District, and not as severe a dress code.

listings.name: Aunt Tiki's
listings.content: Punk version of a tiki bar on Lower Decatur.

listings.name: The Bombay Club
listings.content: High-end cocktails with a dress code.

listings.name: Cafe Lafitte in Exile
listings.content: Claims to be the USA's oldest gay bar ("in exile" since the original Lafitte's (see below) went straight back in the Eisenhower Administration). Everyone welcome.

listings.name: Carousel Bar
listings.content: Renowned for generations for the slowly rotating "Carousel" section; also has non-rotating seating.

listings.name: Crescent City Brewhouse
listings.content: Microbrewery, also serves food.

listings.name: The Dungeon
listings.content: Two dark gothic bars (having split up some ten years ago) open at midnight. The "Original Dungeon" has a bit more cooler atmosphere, but fewer patrons, since it's a little harder to find--down an alley next to "Front of the Dungeon." The Front of the Dungeon's bathroom is a hoot, hidden behind a secret door in the bookcases, and with a toilet so bad as to be borderline unapproachable.

listings.name: Fritzels
listings.content: Best known as a trad jazz venue, but also has a bar with good draft German beer even when there isn't live music.

listings.name: Lafitte's Blacksmith Shop
listings.content: Piano bar towards the end of the touristy part of Bourbon Street, lit entirely by candlelight. Supposedly once the in-town headquarters of pirate & smuggler Jean Lafitte, many colorful stories are told about this location. They pour great Hurricanes.

listings.name: Molly's at the Market
listings.content: A great Irish/Quarterpunk bar, long a favorite of bohemian locals.

listings.name: Molly's On Toulouse
listings.content: A local Irish pub with a pool table & the best juke box in the French Quarter. Irish Car Bombs are $5.50! Great selection of Irish Whiskeys.

listings.name: Napoleon House
listings.content: The place to go if you like the thought of good drinks in a more than 200-year-old building whose owners are proud that the interior hasn't been repainted since World War I, with classical music playing over the sound system. Napoleon never made it here, as he died before the local plan to rescue him from exile and start his empire afresh in Louisiana could be carried out. Napoleon House also serves good sandwiches and a limited food menu, with service at a speed somewhere between leisurely and glacial-- don't stop here if you're in a hurry to be somewhere else.

listings.name: Oz
listings.content: Loud hip gay disco.

listings.name: Parade
listings.content: New Orleans' largest gay nightclub since 1974.

listings.name: Pat O'Brien's
listings.content: Famous for strong Hurricanes, Mint Juleps, TNTs, Purple People Eaters; popular tourist hangout for a reason. Has been trendy for generations. Has an impressive fire/water fountain and patio.

listings.name: Tropical Isle
listings.content: Home of the Hand Grenade, "New Orleans's Most Powerful Drink", is a staple of Bourbon Street decadence. Definitely a must-try.

listings.name: Brieux Carre
listings.content: Small craft brewery located off of Frenchman St. Has a good selection with a primary focus on sours and stouts. Good pilsners.

listings.name: Andrew Jackson Hotel
listings.content: One of the oldest hotels in the French Quarter.

listings.name: Crowne Plaza New Orleans French Quarter
Bienville House
listings.content: Lovely courtyard, pool and balconies

listings.name: Bourbon Orleans
listings.content: Built in 1817.

listings.name: La Galerie Hotel French Quarter
listings.content: This 80-year-old inn offers a complimentary continental breakfast in its elegant lobby.

listings.name: French Market Inn
listings.content: Great location with reasonable rates, it's known for its courtyard atmosphere.

listings.name: Courtyard New Orleans French Quarter/Iberville
listings.content: Caters to business, leisure, family, and is also gay/lesbian friendly. Spacious suites with huge bed, kitchen, large bathroom, living room with fold out, and 2 TVs. Valet parking, free bell-hop, lots of amenities, and free breakfast. They also feature fantastic massages at their spa.

listings.name: Four Points by Sheraton French Quarter
listings.content: A beautiful historic hotel on the site of the old French Opera House. Notable for its balconies overlooking Bourbon and Toulouse Streets and a beautiful courtyard with pool.

listings.name: Holiday Inn Chateau LeMoyne
listings.content: An historic hotel occupying what were four 19th-century townhomes.

listings.name: Lafitte Guest House
listings.content: A boutique hotel in the residential area of Bourbon Street. Visitors will enjoy the sights and sounds of Bourbon Street as well as a retreat into their own personal French Quarter home.

listings.name: Hotel Monteleone
listings.content: In an elegant early-20th century skyscraper (the only one within the confines of the Quarter itself, just constructed just before large new constructions were prohibited here) has long been one of the top upscale Quarter hotels. The hotel includes a rooftop heated pool with views of the skyline and an award-winning restaurant, the Hunt Room Grill.

listings.name: Omni Royal Orleans
listings.content: The Omni Royal Orleans has been a recipient of the AAA four-diamond award for the past 27 years.

listings.name: Royal Barracks Guest House
listings.content: Every room features a queen-sized bed, private bath and fireplace, and private entrance to the courtyard.

listings.name: Hotel Mazarin
listings.content: Luxurious furnishings, with a beautiful courtyard.

listings.name: Hotel St. Pierre
listings.content: Embodies the architecture and ambiance of the 18th-century French Quarter.

listings.name: Ursuline Guest House
listings.content: 13 guest rooms, each with private bath, ceiling fan, air conditioning/heating, cable television and wireless Internet access.

listings.name: Maison Dupuy
listings.content: This hotel has a beautiful courtyard with a real New Orleans atmosphere; renovated historic homes surround what is now the courtyard with a fountain and pool.

listings.name: Hotel Royal
listings.content: On the finest shopping street in the French Quarter, this hotel has a European feeling complemented by authentic laced iron balconies, high ceilings with fans, and enclosed courtyards with fountains.

listings.name: French Quarter Landmark Hotel
listings.content: Within walking distance of the hotel, explore the historic, artistic and eclectic charms around you.

listings.name: Hotel Le Marais
listings.content: A heated saltwater courtyard pool and breakfast area.

listings.name: Place D'Armes
listings.content: Beautiful historic hotel in the quarter. They have interior rooms (no windows) that are a great bargain to stay in an incredible space.

listings.name: Hotel Maison de Ville
listings.content: One of the most historic hotels in the Quarter, everyone from Tennessee Williams to Audobon has spent time there.

listings.name: W New Orleans French Quarter
listings.content: Boutique hotel.

listings.name: City House Hostel
listings.content: Free wireless internet, 24 hour reception. 14 night maximum stay.

listings.name: IHSP French Quarter House
listings.content: Free wireless internet, free breakfast, 24 hour reception. Dorm rooms only open to students and foreign travelers, and there is a 7 night maximum stay.

listings.name: French Quarter Mansion
listings.content: Gay-friendly bed and breakfast in the center of the Quarter.
